FOREWORD

This Indian Standard ( Part 2 ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Rock Mechanics Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division Council. Vertical stress on a rock mass varies in a more predictable former is primarily affected by the weight of overburden. fashion than horizontal stress because the

When an opening is introduced in the rock mass, the natural state of stress The stress around an the rock mass attains a new state of equilibrium. various man-made activities is termed `induced stress' as opposed to virgin The natural state which describes the original, undisturbed state of stress. as in situ stress.

is disturbed locally as opening resulting from stress or absolute stress of stress is often termed

Underground in situ stress is sometimes sufficiently high ( relative to the rock mass strength ) to In such cases, cause rock bursting spelling, buckling, heaving, or other ground control problems. knowledge of the state of in situ stress is of critical importance to the design and construction of engineering structures in a rock mass. Even in cases where the effects of stress are less dramatic, the optimum shape, orientation and layout of under-ground structures, as well as the effectiveness and ultimate cost of rock support systems, can be signrficantly influenced by the in situ stress. Factors affecting the magnitudes and orientation of in situ stress include the weight of overlying and materrals, geologic structures ( on local and regional scales ), tectonic forces within the earth's crust, residual stress and the thermal stress. The complexity of the relations between these factors and In addition, stress cannot be the in situ stress usually prohibits reliable estimatron of rock stress. measured directly, and therefore, rock stress determination techniques rely on the measurement of some response ( e g. displacement, strain, deformation ) that is induced by a disturbance of the This measured response of rock in a stress-disturbed zone ( e g the wall of a tunnel ) rock mass. is extrapolated, from the opening outwards, through a numerical model or analytical techniques; or measurements must be made via a drillhole that extends into an undisturbed region of the rock mass. Several methods have been tried to arrive at a reliable means of measuring in situ stress. offers different advantage and disadvantages with respect to a particular application. Mechanics Sectional Committee has covered following four methods which have got acceptance: Part Part Part Part I 2 3 4 Using the hydraulic Using a USBM-type Using Using fracturing drillhole technique deformation gauge gauges cell with 9 or 12 strain Each Rock wide

In the formulation of this standard due weightage has been given to international co-ordination among the standards and practices prevailing in different countries in addition to relating it to the practices in the field in this country. The technical committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex B.

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the tinal value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rou'nded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised )`. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off values should be the same as that of the specified values in this standard.

IS 13946 ( Part 2 ) : 1994

Indian Standard

DETERMINATION OF ROCK STRESS CODE OF PRACTICE
PART 2 USING 1 SCOPE This standard (Part 2) covers the method of determination of rock stress from measurement of changes in (diameter) deformation of a drillhole during overcoring. The elastic properties of the rock and the deformation measurements are combined to calculate the stresses in the plane perpendicular to the axis of the drillhole. 2 TERMINOLOGY For the porpose of this standard, the definitions in IS 11358 : 1987 shall apply. 3 GENERAL 3.1 For this method to be successful, the rock should not split or fracture during the overcoring process. Thus, it is necessary to obtain cores of a length at least twice the diameter of the overcore. In cases where the core `discs' (e.g. because of very high in situ stresses or thin bedding), modifications to the gauge shall permit testing to continue although alternative means of determining the rock modulus shall be used and corrections shall be applied to the measured diameter changes to account for the proximity to the base of the overcore hole. 3.2 Hole depths usually shall be less than 30 m although measurements to depths of 70 m are made in vertical downholes. 3.3 Stress components in the plane perpendicular to the hole may be evaluated from the results. In tests from ground surface using vertical drillholes, it is common to assume that the vertical stress is equivalent to that imposed by the overburden load. 3.4 In underground situations, tests in a single hole shall be conducted to determine the stresses in a particular plane of interest. Tests from three (or more) non-parallel holes may be analysed by least squares techniques to determine the three dimensional stress components and the standard error associated with the determination. 4 APPARATUS 4.1 Drilling equipment shall include the following: given A USBM-TYPE DRILLHOLE DEFORMATION GAUGE of up to 150 mm dia. The drill shall be capable of running smoothly at about 120 rev/mm while overcoring at a rate of 15-20 mm/mm.

b)

Drill rods and drill bits. The gauge shall be placed in a pilot hole (38 mm dia), which shall be drilled with a single or double-tube core barrel approx 2 m in length. The larger overcoring bit, generally 150 mm dia, may be turned on a BQ wireline drill rod (55.6 mm o.d., 46.0 mm i.d.) or on some equivalent rod whose couplings have a large enough internal diameter to allow free passage of the gauge. Inside the 150 mm dia hole, special stabilizers are required about every 3 m along the drill string to minimize drilling vibrations. The overcoring bit should be chosen carefully so that the diameter of the rock core will fit closely inside the modulus chamber, which will be used later for measuring the elastic modulus of the rock core. In general, the diamater of the overcore should be at least three to four times the diameter of the pilot hole. A water swivel, which connects with the drill rods and permits the passage of the signal cable.

4

Equipment for retrieving cores from the drillhole such as: core-breaking wedge, core shovel, and core puller.

4.2 Equipment for measuring pilot hole diameter changes during overcoring shall include the following: a) A `deformation gauge' suitable for measuring changes in the diameter of the pilot hole in one or more (usually three) orientations. Changes in pilot hole diameter of as little as 1 part in 10 should be detectable. The gauge should be designed so that it is held firmly inside the hole to prevent slippage during the overcoring. It should also be waterproofed and capable of detachment from the signal cable. The USBM gauge, employs cantilever with bonded, electric resistance strain gauges to measure drillhole diameter changes ( see Fig. 1).

a) A diamond

drill to operate with core barrels

IS 13946 ( Part 2 ) : 1994

b) A strain indicator readout bridge and switchgear. c) Placement rods for inserting the deformation gauge inside the pilot hole at depths specified for stress determination. These rods should be marked to show the depth and orientation of the gauge sensors. 4.3 Equipment for ancillary tests shall include the following: a) A calibration device for periodic calibration of the gauge sensors. b) A biaxial modulus chamber with pressure gauge and hand pump for the measurement of the Young's modulus of the large diameter cores. 5 PROCEDURE
5.1 Site Selection

openings; the extent of this zone is generally taken as one diameter (0) of the opening, as indicated in Fig. 2. Four possible drilling configurations are presented in Fig. 2. Configurations (n), (0) and (c) have the advantage that the drill rig does not have to be moved for each hole. Configuration (6) has converging drillholes and, thus, samples the smallest volume of material. 5.2 Drilling,
Gauge Insertion and Overcoring

5.2.1 Unless the stress close to a free is to be studied, actual overcoring of the gauge should not begin until the larger penetrated beyond the influence irregularities or openings.

face of rock deformation drillhole has of surface

5.2.2 Start the hole using the large overcorc bit and drill to the depth at which overcoring is to begin. 5.2.3 Remove the large core and start the pilot hole using a short pilot hole starter core barrel; then, extend the pilot hole for approx 2 m. It is important that the pilot hole remains within +14 mm of the centre of the overcore. Any fracture zones encountered by the pilot hole should be avoided during placing of the instrument. 5.2.4 Iusert the 150 mm core barrel into the drillhole but do not comlect the drill. Thread the gauge readout cable through the drill chuck and special water swivel. 5.2.5 Conect the gauge readout cable to the readout box and take initial readings with the gauge outside

The USBM gauge shall be used to determine the secondary principal stresses (the greatest and the least normal stresses) in the plane perpendicular to the drillhole axis. Therefore, drillhole orientations may be selected to evaluate stress concentrations surrounding underground openings. In cases where the complete stress field is to be calculated at a given location, it is necessary to overcore three non-parallel holes. Deformation measurements should be taken outside the zone of influence of underground openings; the extent of this zone of influence of underground

the hole. Gauge calibration information is normally supplied by the manufacturer. However, direct methods of periodically checking the calibration are available. 5.2.6 Using the placement rods, insert the gauge through the drill rods and into the pilot hole. Orient the gauge so that one cantilever pair lies in a known plane (using a spirit level in horizontal holes or an orientation device on the placement rod in vertical holes). The difference in the rradings should fall within l/2 to 314 of the maximum different range of the cantilevers. If the difference is too small, remove the gauge and add shims to the cantilever contact pistons. If the difference is too large, remove shims. With proper shimming the gauge should fit firmly into the pilot hole without being forced. The cantilever tips should be placed at least 150 mm, and preferably 22.5 mm, past the base of the larger drillhole. This shall ensure that the presence of the larger hole does not significantly affect the in sihl stress field at the point of measurement. 5.2.7 Take up excess slack in the gauge cable and connect the drill stem to the drill. Turn on the drilling water and allowapprox 10 min to elapse before overcoring. This allows the gauge to reach temperature equilibrium. 5.2.8 Start the overcoring with chuck speeds of approx 120 rev/min and a penetration rate of around 20 mm/ min. The water pressure should not fluctuate and should be maintained as low as possible but should be sufficient to allow good clearing of the cuttings. Record the gauge readings on all cantilever axes at every 10 or 20 mm of penetration. A typical field data sheet may be used as Amiex A. 5.2.9 Overcoring should proceed until the overcoring bit had passed over the cantilever tips and beyond, for a distance of at least 150 mm and preferably 225 mm. The total length of overcore is thus 300-450 mm (approx 2-3 times the diameter of the overcore hole). In any case, the overcore should be long enough to obtain gauge readings which do not change with further overcoring.
NO'IX -A secondary diamond drillhole may be made in the vicinity of test hole to locate test zone of 300-4.50 mm length iutact rock and to avoid fracture zones, thus time of test can bc saved substantially.

011 site within 24 h of overcoring. This applies particularly to rock cores which deteriorate with time. Place the rock core inside the modulus chamber so that the actual measurement point is opposite the middle of the chamber. Orient the gauge sensors in the same directions as during the overcoring. Usually, marks are left on the walls of the pilot hole by the buttons of the gauge so that resetting at the correct position and orientation is simplified. If biaxial testing is not to be done soon after overcoring the core should be wrapped and sealed in heavy plastic to prevent drying.

5.3.2 Apply radial pressure to the rock core using the hydraulic hand pump. Record drillhole diameter changes at various increments of applied pressure. Calculate secant values of the biaxial elastic modulus from plots of applied pressure IXVSIIS drillhole diameter changes using the unloading curves. If possible, biaxial test pressures should be selected such that biaxial test deformation magnitudes are comparable to the overcoring deformation magnitudes. However, this is not always possible because the biaxial test does not confine the ends of the core and failure. can occur at relatively low biaxial pressures. Triaxial core testing procedures that minimize the effects of elastic nonlinearity may be used to determine anisotropic elastic parameters. 6 CALCULATIONS

degrees of complexity depending on whether stresses are two- or three - dimensional in character and depending on the degree of elastic aI;isotropy present. 6.2 Where the stress along the drillholc axis is zero (that is stress conditions such as might occur close to the ground surface or close to the wall of an opening), the deformation or change in diameter (v) of the pilot hole shall be given by the equation: u + [ (P+Q)+2(P-Q)

Carefully determine the orientation of the core. Then use the core breaker, core shovel or core puller to remove the ovcrcore. 5.3 Measurement

A further iteration may be performed if so desired. Each set of overcoring data contains three measurements of drillhole diameter change, which are oriented with respect to and to the vertical, plus a value for Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio. All such data sets are treated statistically to yield the least squares estimates of the stress components and their standard error.
